slides.title: Delivery Atlas
slides.speaker: Geremi
slides.script: Good morning. We are Geremi, Anuar, Echenique and Juanro. Our assigned database is ClickHouse. Delivery Atlas is the fictional delivery platform we built to explore its analytical design.

slides.title: A workload for analytical queries
slides.speaker: Geremi
slides.script: Our platform produces customer actions, order changes and courier positions. We verified a mixed run with one hundred fictional customers and fifty couriers. The interval is two seconds. Our question is how to turn an event history into useful views: current deliveries, customer behaviour and historical summaries. The map shows the application; the project explains the ClickHouse tables and queries behind it.

slides.title: A column-oriented SQL database for OLAP
slides.speaker: Geremi
slides.script: ClickHouse is an open-source SQL database designed for analytical processing, or OLAP. Column-oriented storage lets a query read the columns it needs. SQL gives us filters, grouping, joins and aggregate functions. These are different aspects: storage layout does not decide whether a database uses SQL. We therefore describe ClickHouse directly as a column-oriented SQL database, rather than calling it NoSQL simply because it stores columns. It is optimised for analytical reads and batched ingestion. Our demo does not use multi-statement transactions across the outbox and ClickHouse. That is different from saying ClickHouse has no transaction guarantees: some inserts are atomic under documented conditions. Juanro will connect the storage design to one of our queries.

slides.title: The columns behind an analytical query
slides.speaker: Juanro
slides.script: This query groups the Criteo records by treatment and computes the average observed visit label. It needs the treatment and visit columns, rather than all the feature columns. Column storage reduces unnecessary reads for this kind of analysis. MergeTree adds a physical sort order and a sparse index, so a useful filter may skip data granules. New batches create parts, and background merges consolidate them. Compression can also reduce storage and read volume. These are mechanisms, not a promise that every query takes milliseconds. PostgreSQL can use indexes, including index-only scans, so this picture is not a PostgreSQL benchmark. In our project we inspect the actual rows read, server time and query result. The right question is which design answers our workload correctly, with less work.
sources: The displayed two-column query is illustrative. The measured /api/datasets Criteo query also aggregates exposure and conversion; the timing is not attributed to this simplified SQL.

slides.title: The data path into ClickHouse
slides.speaker: Anuar
slides.script: Follow the top path. Fictional events come from rule-based traffic, model decisions and the mini-app. Python validates them and commits accepted events to a local SQLite outbox. The publisher sends batches into delivery_atlas. ClickHouse keeps event histories, while materialized views build aggregate states. The read API merges those states to obtain the latest courier or order. This avoids rebuilding current state from the complete GPS history on every refresh. The lower path is separate: public datasets are loaded into delivery. They support historical questions and retain their own meanings. The outbox helps retry publication after a temporary outage. It does not provide replication, a cross-system transaction or protection against loss of the host disk.

slides.title: Three origins, explicit meanings
slides.speaker: Anuar
slides.script: We distinguish three origins. Rule-based traffic generates repeatable fictional activity. Model-controlled customers make bounded decisions through a local model, and Python validates the results. Downloaded sources contain public observations, such as Criteo user records and Glovo catalog entries. All generated customers, purchases and GPS positions remain fictional, including those controlled by the model. The current hybrid configuration assigns three customers to the model and ninety-seven to traffic. A customer appears in the AI metrics after a model decision is recorded, so configuration alone is not proof that it acted. Public records are not joined to our fictional customer journeys. In particular, Glovo catalog size measures supply, and the released Criteo sample supports observed group summaries, not recovery of the original campaign incrementality.

slides.title: The map reads current state
slides.speaker: Echenique
slides.script: We now switch to the dashboard. These are real Madrid street tiles, with fictional couriers and GPS samples. I select one courier and follow its order. The latest position comes from a ClickHouse latest-state view using argMax aggregate states. The recorded path is a separate read of that courier's history. The line joins recorded samples; it is not a road-routing result. The browser polls periodically, and cached reads reduce duplicate work for viewers. I check the event time and position age before describing anything as current. Polling every two seconds does not guarantee two-second end-to-end freshness. If this is the recorded fallback, I will say so explicitly.

slides.title: Read each view in its own scope
slides.speaker: Echenique
slides.script: First I select AI agents and inspect a recorded decision. In our verification the model had reached its limit of one hundred and twenty calls. Traffic was still running, so moving couriers did not prove that the model was still deciding. Then I switch to downloaded datasets. Our Criteo read processed thirteen million nine hundred and seventy-nine thousand five hundred and ninety-two rows in one hundred and five point seven milliseconds of ClickHouse execution time. This is one dated observation of the endpoint query, not a benchmark against another database or a guaranteed latency. I report the current timestamp and rows read with the time. The released sample supports observed group summaries. Server time excludes browser and gateway latency, and a shared response can be cached.

slides.title: Implemented, awaiting deployment, next checks
slides.speaker: Juanro
slides.script: The core event path and map are implemented. The public-data views are separate from fictional activity. Customer Journey and ClickHouse Performance are already implemented in PR nine, with tests; the next step is deployment, not starting their development. Anuar reports that his host is still on main seven-three-four-three-seven-four-d, which does not contain those routes. Before the final talk we need the backend and gateway updated together, a prepared CRUD demonstration on a scratch table, an independent installation check and a timed rehearsal. The main limits remain one node, finite model calls and dependence on the host and tunnel. ReplacingMergeTree replacement happens during merges or at query time with FINAL. It does not enforce a unique key or automatically repair aggregates fed by duplicate inserts.

slides.title: ClickHouse in practice
slides.speaker: Geremi
slides.script: Our main lesson is to connect each analytical question to its data grain, storage design and measured query cost. Delivery Atlas makes those choices visible. Thank you. We are ready for your questions.
